#| label: setup

library(tidymodels)

## Why this matters

[Maximum likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd) has one blind spot, and it is serious. It
considers only the data in front of it. If forty stations happen to suggest that abundance
rises by 8.6 individuals per standard deviation of temperature and falls by 6.2 per squared
standard deviation, maximum likelihood will report those numbers, because they are the ones
that make those forty stations most probable.

You know that is wrong. Not from the data — from everything else you know about the species.
Effects that large do not occur; a pair of coefficients that huge and opposite is two
collinear terms fighting, not biology.

**Maximum a posteriori** estimation is the machinery for saying so. And the reason it appears
in a machine-learning course, rather than only a Bayesian statistics course, is that it turns
out to be the same calculation as ridge regression — a technique
[section 5](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) will present with no mention of priors at
all.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## The idea

### Adding a second term

Maximum likelihood maximises $\log p(\text{data} \mid \theta)$. MAP maximises that plus one
more term: how plausible the parameters themselves are, before any data arrived.

$$\hat\theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_\theta \; \underbrace{\log p(y \mid \theta)}_{\text{what the data say}} \; + \; \underbrace{\log p(\theta)}_{\text{what you knew}}$$

$p(\theta)$ is the **prior**. It is not a statement of certainty; it is a statement of scale.
"Coefficients of this model are typically within about ±1, occasionally ±2, essentially never
±9" is a prior, and it is a claim you can defend from the literature.

The result is a compromise, and where the compromise lands is governed by which term is more
confident. Strong data overwhelm a vague prior; weak data get pulled towards it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-prior-likelihood
#| fig-cap: "Prior, likelihood and posterior for the temperature coefficient, from the forty-station fit below. The likelihood (grey) peaks at 8.59 but is very wide — the standard error is 5.95, so the data barely distinguish 8.59 from zero. As the prior tightens from left to right, the posterior peak is dragged towards zero: 3.56, then 0.31, then 0.06."
#| fig-alt: "Three side-by-side panels, each showing three curves against a coefficient axis from minus 5 to 15. In every panel a broad flat grey curve peaks at 8.59, representing the likelihood. A prior curve centred on zero narrows from panel to panel, and a posterior curve sits between the two. In the left panel, with the widest prior, the posterior peaks near 3.6. In the middle panel it peaks just above zero. In the right panel, with the narrowest prior, the posterior is almost indistinguishable from the prior and peaks at 0.06."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
b_hat <- 8.590   # temperature coefficient from the 40-station fit
se    <- 5.950   # its standard error

curves <- map_dfr(c(5.0, 1.146, 0.5), \(tau) {
  b <- seq(-5, 15, length.out = 500)
  post_mode <- b_hat * tau^2 / (tau^2 + se^2)
  post_sd   <- sqrt(1 / (1 / se^2 + 1 / tau^2))
  tibble(
    b,
    Likelihood = dnorm(b, b_hat, se),
    Prior      = dnorm(b, 0, tau),
    Posterior  = dnorm(b, post_mode, post_sd),
    panel = factor(sprintf("prior sd = %.2f  →  peak at %.2f", tau, post_mode),
                   levels = sprintf("prior sd = %.2f  →  peak at %.2f",
                                    c(5.0, 1.146, 0.5),
                                    b_hat * c(5.0, 1.146, 0.5)^2 /
                                      (c(5.0, 1.146, 0.5)^2 + se^2)))
  )
}) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Likelihood, Prior, Posterior), names_to = "curve", values_to = "density")

ggplot(curves, aes(b, density, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    Likelihood = ml_palette[["grey"]],
    Prior      = ml_palette[["orange"]],
    Posterior  = ml_palette[["blue"]]
  )) +
  labs(x = "Temperature coefficient", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "Prior × likelihood = posterior") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

The middle panel is the honest description of what a modest prior does to a badly determined
coefficient: it removes almost all of it. The data never really supported 8.59 — the standard
error says so — and the prior is simply refusing to pretend otherwise.

::: {.callout-note}
This figure treats the temperature coefficient one at a time, holding the others fixed. The
joint fit below gives 0.329 where the single-coefficient calculation gives 0.307, because the
other eleven coefficients are being shrunk at the same time. The picture is the right picture;
the third decimal is illustrative.
:::

### The step that matters for machine learning

Choose a Normal prior centred at zero, with standard deviation $\tau$, and write out what MAP
is maximising. The log of a Normal density is a negative squared term, so

$$\log p(y \mid \beta) + \log p(\beta) \;=\; -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2 \;-\; \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\sum_j \beta_j^2 + \text{const}$$

Multiply through by $-2\sigma^2$ and maximising becomes minimising

$$\sum_i (y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j \beta_j^2, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}$$

That is **ridge regression**, exactly. The penalty is not a computational trick invented to
stabilise a matrix inverse; it is a Normal prior on the coefficients, and $\lambda$ is the
ratio of how noisy you think the data are to how large you think the effects are.

Swap the prior and you get a different penalty:

| Prior on each coefficient | Penalty it becomes | Method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal(0, τ) | $\lambda\sum \beta_j^2$ | Ridge |
| Laplace(0, b) | $\lambda\sum \lvert\beta_j\rvert$ | Lasso |
| Mixture of the two | Both terms | Elastic net |
| Flat (improper) | None | Maximum likelihood |

The last row is the point. Maximum likelihood is not the neutral, assumption-free default it
feels like. It is MAP with a prior that considers a coefficient of 900 exactly as plausible as
a coefficient of 0.9.

## Worked example

We will take forty stations — a realistic size for a pilot survey — twelve predictors, and
compare the unpenalised fit with the MAP fit.

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

d <- survey |>
  select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3,
         salinity_psu, substrate, season) |>
  drop_na()

X <- scale(model.matrix(
  ~ depth_m + I(depth_m^2) + temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2) +
    chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season,
  data = d
)[, -1])
y <- d$abundance - mean(d$abundance)

train_rows <- sample(nrow(d), 40)
X_train <- X[train_rows, ];  y_train <- y[train_rows]
X_test  <- X[-train_rows, ]; y_test  <- y[-train_rows]

c(stations_training = nrow(X_train), predictors = ncol(X_train),
  stations_testing = nrow(X_test))
```

```{r}
#| label: map-equals-ridge
sigma <- 4.5      # assumed noise scale, individuals
tau   <- 1.146    # prior sd on the coefficients

neg_log_posterior <- function(b) {
  -sum(dnorm(y_train, X_train %*% b, sigma, log = TRUE)) -
    sum(dnorm(b, 0, tau, log = TRUE))
}

map_fit <- optim(rep(0, ncol(X_train)), neg_log_posterior, method = "BFGS",
                 control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 10000))

ridge_closed_form <- function(lambda) {
  drop(solve(t(X_train) %*% X_train + lambda * diag(ncol(X_train)),
             t(X_train) %*% y_train))
}

tibble(
  term  = colnames(X_train),
  MLE   = ridge_closed_form(0),
  MAP   = map_fit$par,
  ridge = ridge_closed_form(sigma^2 / tau^2)
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

The MAP column and the ridge column agree to eight decimal places. They are not similar
procedures; they are the same arithmetic reached from two directions.

Look at the MLE column while you are here. Temperature gets +8.59 and its square −6.20; depth
gets +1.04 and its square −1.78. Those pairs are not estimates of anything — they are two
nearly collinear terms taking large opposite values that partly cancel. MAP reports +0.33 and
−0.16 for the same pair.

### Does it predict better?

```{r}
#| label: lambda-curve
rmse <- function(b, X, y) sqrt(mean((y - X %*% b)^2))

lambdas <- exp(seq(log(0.01), log(500), length.out = 120))

curve <- tibble(lambda = lambdas) |>
  mutate(
    b      = map(lambda, ridge_closed_form),
    train  = map_dbl(b, rmse, X = X_train, y = y_train),
    test   = map_dbl(b, rmse, X = X_test,  y = y_test),
    largest_coefficient = map_dbl(b, \(v) max(abs(v)))
  )

curve |>
  filter(lambda %in% lambdas[c(1, 40, 60, 75, 90, 120)]) |>
  select(lambda, largest_coefficient, train, test) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-lambda
#| fig-cap: "Training and test error against the prior strength λ, for the forty-station fit. Training error rises steadily as the prior tightens — the fit to the forty stations can only get worse. Test error falls to a minimum near λ = 15 and then rises again. The horizontal line is the error from predicting the overall mean at every station."
#| fig-alt: "Two curves against lambda from 0.01 to 500 on a logarithmic horizontal axis, with root mean squared error from 3.2 to 5 on the vertical axis. The training curve starts at 3.32 and rises smoothly to about 4.2 at the right-hand edge. The test curve starts at 4.75, dips to a minimum of 4.50 near lambda 15, then rises back above 4.7. A dashed horizontal line at 4.85 marks the error of predicting the mean, which sits above both curves everywhere."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.3
curve |>
  select(lambda, Training = train, Test = test) |>
  pivot_longer(-lambda, names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(lambda, rmse, colour = set)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = sqrt(mean(y_test^2)), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "λ — prior strength (log scale)", y = "RMSE (individuals)", colour = NULL,
    title = "A prior is not a cost, it is an investment",
    subtitle = "Dashed line: predicting the mean everywhere"
  )
```

## What the results mean

The unpenalised fit — the one that makes these forty stations most probable — achieves a test
RMSE of 4.745. Predicting the overall mean at every station achieves 4.850. Maximum likelihood
on forty stations and twelve predictors bought about 2% over a model with no predictors at all.

With a prior of the right strength, the same data and the same twelve predictors give 4.495 —
more than three times the improvement, from adding a term that contains no data whatsoever.

The shape of the two curves is the whole lesson of the next section, arriving early:

- **Training error rises monotonically with λ.** It must. Every unit of prior pulls the fit
  away from the point that best matches the training stations. A model that fits your data
  worse is what you are buying.
- **Test error falls, then rises.** Up to about λ = 15 the shrinkage removes more noise than
  signal. Past it, real effects start being flattened too, and by λ = 200 the model is barely
  better than the mean.
- **You cannot pick λ from the training curve.** It has no minimum. This is precisely why
  [hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) needs held-out
  data, and why λ is a hyperparameter rather than a parameter.

Notice also what shrinkage does *not* do. Salinity — which has no effect at all in this
simulation — gets 0.88 from maximum likelihood and still 0.54 from MAP. A Normal prior pulls
coefficients towards zero but never to zero, so ridge cannot tell you a variable is irrelevant.
That is the Laplace prior's job, and lasso's, in
[section 5](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning}
Ridge and lasso penalise coefficients on the scale they are measured on, so a predictor in
millimetres is penalised a thousand times more lightly than the same predictor in metres. The
prior reading makes this obvious — "coefficients are around ±1" is meaningless without knowing
what a unit is — and it is why every penalised fit must standardise its predictors first. The
example above scales `X` before doing anything else.
:::

## Where this breaks down

**A prior can be wrong, and then it hurts.** Everything above assumed effects are centred on
zero and modest. If your species really does have a threshold response with a huge
coefficient, a tight prior will shrink a real effect and you will conclude, confidently, that
it is not there. Priors are assumptions; they belong in the methods section with the rest.

**MAP is a point, not a posterior.** It reports the single most probable parameter value and
discards the shape of the distribution around it. A genuinely Bayesian analysis keeps the whole
posterior, which is what lets it quote intervals honestly. MAP is the cheap corner of Bayesian
inference — you get the shrinkage without the uncertainty — and you should not describe a
ridge fit as a Bayesian analysis.

**Choosing λ from the data is not a prior.** Selecting λ by cross-validation, which is what
everyone does and what section 5 will teach, means the "prior" was read off the data. It works
well and it is standard practice, but it is no longer a statement of prior belief, and the
resulting intervals are optimistic for the same reason any twice-used dataset is.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points

- **MAP** maximises the likelihood plus a prior: what the data say, plus what you knew about
  the size of plausible effects.
- A Normal prior on the coefficients **is** ridge regression, with $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$
  — verified here to eight decimal places. A Laplace prior is lasso.
- Maximum likelihood is therefore not assumption-free; it is MAP with a prior that finds any
  coefficient equally plausible.
- On forty stations and twelve predictors, unpenalised fitting beat predicting the mean by 2%;
  the MAP fit beat it by 7%.
- Training error rises monotonically with the prior strength while test error is U-shaped. The
  training curve cannot choose λ for you.

:::

## Try it yourself

1. Change `sigma` from 4.5 to 9 and refit, leaving `tau` alone. Predict first what should
   happen to the coefficients, then check — and explain the direction in terms of the two
   things λ is a ratio of.
2. Replace the Normal prior in `neg_log_posterior()` with a Laplace one
   (`-sum(abs(b)) / scale` plus a constant) and refit. Do any coefficients reach exactly zero?
   `optim()` will struggle at the kink — what does that tell you about why lasso needs a
   different algorithm?
